title: isClub_univ: The Top of the Club Filter
content:
The whole space $\kappa.\text{ord}$ (here `Set.univ`) is a club. Closedness is trivial — every ordinal belongs to `univ`. Unboundedness uses that $\kappa.\text{ord}$ is a limit ordinal: since $\kappa \geq \aleph_0$, `isSuccLimit_ord` makes $\kappa.\text{ord}$ a successor-limit, so for any $\alpha < \kappa.\text{ord}$ the successor $\alpha+1$ is again below $\kappa.\text{ord}$ and strictly above $\alpha$.

This is the top element $\top$ of the club filter: it is the largest club, and its presence is what makes the club filter a filter on the full power set of $\kappa.\text{ord}$.
mathContext: $\kappa.\text{ord} \in \text{Club}(\kappa)$; equivalently the club filter is a filter on $\mathcal{P}(\kappa.\text{ord})$ with top element the whole space

title: inter_isClosedBelow: Closedness is Preserved
content:
If $C$ and $D$ are closed below $\kappa.\text{ord}$, so is $C \cap D$. The proof is purely formal: a point $\gamma$ that is cofinal-approached from inside $C \cap D$ is in particular cofinal-approached from inside $C$ (every witness $\delta \in C \cap D$ lies in $C$) and from inside $D$, so closedness of each factor places $\gamma$ in both.

This is the easy half of the binary-intersection theorem; all the real work is in unboundedness.
mathContext: $\text{closed}(C) \wedge \text{closed}(D) \Rightarrow \text{closed}(C \cap D)$; in the order topology this is just 'an intersection of closed sets is closed'

title: inter_isUnbounded: Interleaving Two Clubs into One ω-Chain
content:
This is the heart of the file. Given $\alpha_0 < \kappa.\text{ord}$ we must find a point of $C \cap D$ above $\alpha_0$. The construction builds **one** increasing $\omega$-chain that visits both clubs alternately:

$$\alpha_0 < c_0 < d_0 < c_1 < d_1 < \cdots, \qquad c_n \in C,\ d_n \in D.$$

Concretely `cElt` uses unboundedness of $C$ to step strictly above the current point into $C$, and `dElt` then steps above that $c$ into $D$. The recursion `seq` records the $d$-values as the main sequence $s$, carrying along the proof that each term is $< \kappa.\text{ord}$ (a subtype `{α // α < κ.ord}`), and `cElt (seq n)` is the intermediate $C$-point with $s_n < c_n < s_{n+1}$.

Regularity is used **once**, decisively: `iSup_lt_ord_lift_of_isRegular` bounds the supremum $\gamma = \bigsqcup_n s_n$ strictly below $\kappa.\text{ord}$ — an $\omega$-indexed sup of ordinals below a regular uncountable $\kappa.\text{ord}$ stays below it.

The payoff: $\gamma$ is approached cofinally from inside $C$ (by the $c_n$) **and** from inside $D$ (by the $d_n = s_{n+1}$). Closedness of $C$ forces $\gamma \in C$; closedness of $D$ forces $\gamma \in D$. Hence $\gamma \in C \cap D$ and $\gamma > \alpha_0$.
mathContext: For clubs $C, D$ and any $\alpha_0 < \kappa.\text{ord}$ there is $\gamma \in C \cap D$ with $\alpha_0 < \gamma < \kappa.\text{ord}$; the supremum of the interleaved chain is the witness (Jech, Set Theory, Theorem 8.3)

title: Carrying the Bound Through the Recursion
content:
A subtle but essential design choice: the sequence is built valued in the subtype $\{\alpha : \text{Ordinal} \mid \alpha < \kappa.\text{ord}\}$, not in raw ordinals. Each step `step t = ⟨dElt t, dElt_lt t⟩` packages the next ordinal **together with** a proof it stays below $\kappa.\text{ord}$, so the recursion `seq : ℕ → {α // α < κ.ord}` never loses the bound. The projection `s n = (seq n).val` then satisfies `s n < κ.ord` definitionally via `(seq n).prop`.

The definitional equality `s (n+1) = dElt (seq n)` (true by `rfl`) is what lets the $D$-membership argument use `dElt_mem (seq n)` directly for the term $s(n+1)$, and lets the strict-increase `s n < cElt (seq n) < s (n+1)` chain together. This mirrors the parent's `diagInter_isUnbounded`, where the same subtype technique tames the $\kappa$-indexed bump function.
mathContext: The construction stays inside $\kappa.\text{ord}$ at every finite stage; only the limit $\gamma$ requires regularity to remain below $\kappa.\text{ord}$

title: inter_isClub: Binary Intersection Closure
content: Combining `inter_isUnbounded` and `inter_isClosedBelow` gives the headline result: the intersection of two clubs is a club. In filter language, $\text{Club}(\kappa)$ is closed under binary intersection — the defining property of a filter base.

title: isClub_biInter: Finite Intersection of Clubs
content:
By induction on a `Finset` of indices, $\bigcap_{i \in t} C_i$ is a club whenever each $C_i$ is. The empty case is `isClub_univ` (the empty intersection is the whole space); the `insert` case rewrites $\bigcap_{i \in \text{insert } a\, s} C_i = C_a \cap \bigcap_{i \in s} C_i$ via `Finset.set_biInter_insert` and applies `inter_isClub`.

This is the precise statement that the clubs are closed under **finite** intersection — i.e. they form a filter base generating the proper filter $\text{Club}(\kappa)$.
mathContext: For a finite index set $t$, $(\forall i \in t,\ \text{club}(C_i)) \Rightarrow \text{club}\big(\bigcap_{i \in t} C_i\big)$

title: IsNonStationary: The Dual Ideal NS(κ)
content:
A set $S$ is **nonstationary** if it is disjoint from some club: $\exists C,\ \text{club}(C) \wedge S \cap C = \varnothing$. The nonstationary sets are exactly the members of the dual ideal $\text{NS}(\kappa)$ of the club filter — the 'small' or 'negligible' sets from the club filter's point of view.

The definition packages 'disjoint from some club' as $\forall \alpha \in S,\ \alpha \notin C$, which is the form most convenient for the ideal-closure proofs.
mathContext: $S \in \text{NS}(\kappa) \iff \exists C \in \text{Club}(\kappa),\ S \cap C = \varnothing$; $\text{NS}(\kappa)$ is the ideal dual to the club filter

title: isStationary_iff_not_isNonStationary: The Duality
content:
The exact sense in which 'stationary = not in the dual ideal': $\text{IsStationary}\,\kappa\,S \iff \neg\,\text{IsNonStationary}\,\kappa\,S$.

This is a De Morgan / double-negation identity rather than new mathematics. 'Stationary' means *meets every club* ($\forall C,\ S \cap C \neq \varnothing$); 'nonstationary' means *misses some club* ($\exists C,\ S \cap C = \varnothing$). These are literal negations of one another, and the parent's `not_isStationary_iff` supplies the bridge. The genuine content of the filter/ideal theory therefore lives in the closure theorems (`inter_isClub`, `isNonStationary_union`), not in this restatement.
mathContext: $S$ stationary $\iff S \notin \text{NS}(\kappa)$; the stationary sets are the $\text{Club}(\kappa)$-positive sets, the complement of the dual ideal

title: isNonStationary_union: Where the Filter Meets the Ideal
content:
The nonstationary ideal is closed under binary union — and this is the one ideal axiom whose proof genuinely uses the club-filter structure. If $S$ avoids the club $C$ and $T$ avoids the club $D$, then $S \cup T$ avoids the club $C \cap D$ (a club by `inter_isClub`): any $\alpha \in S \cup T$ landing in $C \cap D$ would, if in $S$, contradict $S \cap C = \varnothing$, and if in $T$, contradict $T \cap D = \varnothing$.

This is the precise dual of finite-intersection closure for the filter: $\bigcap$ on the filter side ↔ $\bigcup$ on the ideal side. Together with downward closure (`isNonStationary_subset`) and $\varnothing \in \text{NS}(\kappa)$ (`isNonStationary_empty`), it certifies that $\text{NS}(\kappa)$ is a genuine ideal.
mathContext: $S, T \in \text{NS}(\kappa) \Rightarrow S \cup T \in \text{NS}(\kappa)$, witnessed by the club $C \cap D$; dual to $\text{Club}(\kappa)$ being closed under $\cap$

title: isStationary_univ: Properness of the Filter
content:
The whole space is stationary: every club is nonempty (its unboundedness at $0 < \kappa.\text{ord}$ produces a member), so it meets `univ`. Equivalently, $\varnothing \notin \text{Club}(\kappa)$ — the club filter is **proper**, and $\text{univ} \notin \text{NS}(\kappa)$.

The small lemma $0 < \kappa.\text{ord}$ comes from $\omega = \aleph_0.\text{ord} \leq \kappa.\text{ord}$ (monotonicity of `ord`) together with $0 < \omega$. Properness is what distinguishes a filter of 'large' sets from the degenerate filter containing $\varnothing$, and it is the final piece certifying that $(\text{Club}(\kappa), \text{NS}(\kappa))$ is a non-trivial filter/ideal pair.
mathContext: $\text{univ}$ is stationary, so $\varnothing \notin \text{Club}(\kappa)$: the club filter is a proper filter on $\kappa.\text{ord}$
